content: A Ulysses pact is a decision made voluntarily by an individual with the specific intention of binding themselves to a particular course of action or restriction in the future. This concept is frequently discussed in the field of medicine, particularly in the context of advance directives or living wills. These are legal documents in which a person outlines their preferences for medical treatment in case they become unable to make decisions for themselves. However, there is ongoing debate about whether a decision made by an individual in one state of health should remain binding when that person is in a significantly different, often worse, state of health. The term Ulysses pact originates from the story of Ulysses (known as Odysseus in Greek mythology) and his encounter with the Sirens during his journey. Ulysses, aware of the irresistible and dangerous allure of the Sirens' song, wanted to experience it without succumbing to its fatal consequences. To achieve this, he devised a plan: he instructed his crew to plug their ears with wax so they would not hear the song and to tie him securely to the mast of the ship. He explicitly ordered them not to alter their course under any circumstances, even if he begged or commanded them to do so. Furthermore, he directed them to use their weapons against him if he managed to break free from his restraints. When the ship approached the Sirens, Ulysses heard their song and was overcome by an uncontrollable desire to join them, which would have led to his death. He temporarily lost his rationality and struggled with all his strength to escape his bonds. However, his crew, following his prior instructions, kept him restrained and ensured the ship safely passed the Sirens' domain.
